    Diagram Component Palette

    Click elements to instantiate them onto the architecture canvas window.

    Process / Service
    Process Component
    Functional Definition:
    Any active computational engine, runtime application container, execution node, or microservice block running business instructions software.
    Data Store
    Data Store Component
    Functional Definition:
    Any persistence layer, ledger engine, cluster directory, hardware disk partition, or caching cluster storing persistent or volatile system state data.
    External Entity
    External Entity Component
    Functional Definition:
    An untrusted origin consumer, client terminal, or downstream partner framework sitting outside system cluster firewall configurations.
    Trust Boundary Zone
    Trust Boundary Zone
    Functional Definition:
    A structural border isolation box grouping items together where privilege access levels or trust shifting context boundaries change.
    Trust Boundary Line
    Trust Boundary Line
    Functional Definition:
    A linear segment indicating a change in trust, privilege levels, or security protocols between distinct architectural layers.

    Threat actor
    Threat actor (external entity)
    Attack-path entry:
    An external entity preset for the attacker. Like every external entity it is an entry point for Insights → Attack paths, and it gets threats and suggestions as usual.
    Crown jewel
    Crown jewel (data store)
    Attack-path target:
    A data store marked as a crown jewel: the asset an attacker is after. Insights → Attack paths ranks the routes that reach it.
    Entry point
    Entry point
    Attack tree / flow:
    Where the attacker gets in: an exposed service, a phishing mail, a stolen laptop. A diagram shape, not a system component.
    Attack step
    Attack step (action)
    MITRE Attack Flow action:
    One thing the attacker does. Pick its ATT&CK tactic and, optionally, a technique ID such as T1566 in Properties; both are shown on the shape.
    Asset / target
    Asset / target
    MITRE Attack Flow asset:
    Something an attack step acts on or gains: an account, a host, a secret, a data set.
    Condition / outcome
    Condition / outcome
    MITRE Attack Flow condition:
    A state the attack depends on or produces. Mark it as success or fail in Properties.
    AND gate
    AND gate
    Attack tree operator:
    The parent goal is reached only when ALL child steps succeed. Connect the children to the gate and the gate to its parent.
    OR gate
    OR gate
    Attack tree operator:
    The parent goal is reached when ANY one of the child steps succeeds.
    Goal
    Goal (attack-tree root)
    Attack tree root:
    What the attacker ultimately wants, at the top of the tree: “Read customer data”, “Stop payments”.
    Countermeasure
    Countermeasure / defence
    Attack-defence tree:
    A defence that stops or detects a step. Connect it to the step it counters.
    Choke point
    Choke point
    Attack-path marker:
    A place many attack paths pass through: one control here cuts several routes.

    Step Activity
    Step Activity Component
    Functional Definition:
    An indexable timeline sequence node used to illustrate sequential activities, data flows, or multi-step user interaction journeys.
    Comment Textbox
    Comment Textbox
    Functional Definition:
    A documentation utility block to add descriptive metadata, assumptions, or operational context notes onto specific canvas regions.
    Canvas Headline
    Canvas Headline
    Functional Definition:
    A stylized text display label used to organize architecture charts into clear visual blocks or create master banners.
    Table
    Table
    Functional Definition:
    A grid of text cells with an optional header row and header column, in the swimlane colours. Add or remove rows and columns and edit the cells in Properties.

    Custom Image / Icon
    Custom Graphic Image
    Functional Definition:
    Allows importing custom graphic elements, system logos, or specific icons directly onto the diagram. Supports loading local files or web URLs.
    Infrastructure Node
    Infrastructure Component
    Functional Definition:
    Any physical or virtual hardware server, security appliance, network switch, router, firewall, or email broker mapping infrastructure layers.

    Swimlane Grid Layout
    Swimlane Grid Layout
    Functional Definition:
    A dynamic matrix grid component that automatically groups, bounds, and resizes relative to elements placed inside its cells. Supports adding/deleting rows and columns.
    Pool (Horizontal Lanes)
    Pool (Horizontal Lanes)
    Functional Definition:
    A BPMN-style pool: a vertical title band on the left and horizontal lanes for each participant. Shapes placed inside move with it. Add, remove and rename lanes in Properties.
    Vertical Lanes
    Vertical Lanes
    Functional Definition:
    Side-by-side columns with a header each, for teams, systems or stages. Shapes placed inside move with it. Add, remove and rename columns in Properties.
    Group / Frame
    Group / Frame
    Functional Definition:
    A titled box that groups related shapes. It is drawn behind them and carries them along when moved. Not a trust zone.
    Phases / Timeline
    Phases / Timeline
    Functional Definition:
    Columns as phases with arrow-shaped headers, for a timeline or a delivery process. Add, remove and rename phases in Properties.
    Process (Rectangle)
    □ Process (Rectangle)
    Flowchart Definition:
    Represents a step or action in a process. The standard rectangular symbol used for any general operation or task.
    Decision (Diamond)
    ◆ Decision (Diamond)
    Flowchart Definition:
    Represents a decision point with branching paths (Yes/No, True/False). A diamond shape indicating a conditional check.
    Terminator (Oval)
    ◯ Terminator (Oval)
    Flowchart Definition:
    Marks the Start or End point of a process flow. A rounded stadium/pill shape used at the beginning and termination of a flowchart.
    Data / I-O
    ▱ Data / I-O
    Flowchart Definition:
    Represents input or output data. A parallelogram indicating data entering or leaving a process step.
    Document
    📄 Document
    Flowchart Definition:
    Represents a document or report produced or used by a process. Has a rectangular top and a wavy bottom edge.
    Manual Input
    ▩ Manual Input
    Flowchart Definition:
    Represents a step where data is manually entered by a person. A trapezoid with a slanted top edge indicating keyboard or form input.
    Preparation (Hexagon)
    ⬡ Preparation
    Flowchart Definition:
    Represents initialization or preparatory steps, such as setting a loop counter. A hexagon with pointed left and right sides.
    Connector (Circle)
    ◯ Connector
    Flowchart Definition:
    A small circle used as an on-page or off-page connector to link separate sections of a flowchart, avoiding long crossing lines.
    Stored Data
    ⌨ Stored Data
    Flowchart Definition:
    Represents data stored somewhere in a system — on disk, memory, or a file. A rounded-right D-shaped symbol.
    3D shapes
    Sphere
    Sphere
    3D shape:
    A shaded ball, for a node, a cluster, a planet-style overview or anything that should stand out. Drawn as a solid in the flat and isometric views.
    Cone
    Cone
    3D shape:
    A cone on a round base, for a funnel, a filter or an entry point. Drawn as a solid in the flat and isometric views.
    Pyramid
    Pyramid
    3D shape:
    A square pyramid, for a hierarchy, a privilege level or a tiered model. Drawn as a solid in the flat and isometric views.
    Stacked layers
    Stacked layers
    3D shape:
    Three stacked slabs, for platform layers, a technology stack or defence in depth. Drawn as a solid in the flat and isometric views.

        Live status

        Colour shapes and flows by live data: a Google Sheet, a CSV or JSON feed, or a check the browser runs itself (web address, reachability, DNS). Turn on Status check in a shape's or flow's Properties to choose its rules. Sources and rules are saved in the model; results stay in this tab. Nothing is contacted until you allow its host here.

        Allow live status to contact these hosts?
          Your browser sends a request (with its IP address, but no cookies) to each host every refresh. A DNS check sends the host name to the DNS provider. Only allow hosts you trust; a model from someone else may name any host.
          Status sources in this model
          A file next to the app (like samples/status-servers.csv) needs no approval. Google Sheets: share it as "Anyone with the link can view" and paste that link (a "Publish to web" link redirects, and redirects are not followed). The first row is the header row.
          A column by its header, letter (B) or number (2). A column called "latency" is used by latency rules.
          A list like [{"name": "API", "status": "up", "latency": 120}] or a map like {"API": "up"}.
          Allowed hosts in this browser

          Browsers cannot ping (ICMP): Reachability sends a small HTTPS request and times the reply. Without CORS on the server a web check can only tell that the host answered, not its status code. Plain http:// addresses are blocked by the app's security policy.

          Git sync (GitHub / GitLab)

          Save this model to a file in a repository and load it from there with the sync button next to ☰. Server, repository, branch and file are saved in the model and its exports, so a colleague only needs their own token. The token stays in this browser, encrypted with your passphrase. Sync sends the model to the server you enter here.

          A Markdown file that GitHub and GitLab show as a page with the diagram drawn; README.md is the repository's front page. It is written fresh on every sync and never read back, so it replaces any file with that name and changes made to it in the repository are overwritten.
          Include in the readable copy
          GitHub: a fine-grained token for this repository with Contents: Read and write. GitLab: a personal or project access token with the api scope. Leave empty to keep the token already saved for this server.
          Unlock git sync

          • Keep mine saves this model over the repository copy (git history keeps the old one).
          • Take theirs loads the repository copy; this model is saved in History first.
          About & License v

          Threat Tiger is an offline-first threat-modelling tool: draw your system as a data-flow diagram, mark the trust boundaries, and get concrete threats (STRIDE) from a curated library, ranked by what your model shows. Everything stays in this browser.

          New here? The Help guide walks through every part of the app, with pictures. Open it any time from ☰ → Help or with F1.

          Third-party icons: the icon sets come from AWS, Microsoft (Azure, Entra, Fluent UI), Google Cloud, the Kubernetes project, Devicon and Simple Icons.           Welcome to Threat Tiger

          Draw your system, let the tiger point out what could go wrong, and keep track of what you will do about it. Everything stays in your browser.

          Start here

          Getting started: your first model in five steps

          1. Draw the parts of your system. In the left panel, click (or drag) a Process / Service, a Data Store and an External Entity onto the canvas. Rename each one in Properties → Component Label; the field suggests names that fit the type.
          2. Connect them with data flows. Hover a shape until its small connection points appear, then drag from a point to another shape. Each line is a data flow: who sends what to whom.
          3. Describe the security. Drag a Trust Boundary Zone around the parts you control (for example your cloud network). Select a flow and switch on Encrypted or Authenticated where that is true; set switches such as Stores PII on the data store.
          4. Find the threats. Select a component and open the Threat Templates tab. Suggestions triggered by your model (an unencrypted flow across a boundary, a store with personal data…) are listed first, with the reason. Click Add on the ones that apply.
          5. Decide what to do. In the Active Threat Register at the bottom, rate each threat (likelihood × impact), set its status and link Mitigations. Insights shows what is still open, and ☰ → Print report… or Export Markdown report produces the write-up.

          Start here

          Threat modelling in a nutshell

          Threat modelling means looking at how a system is built and asking “what could go wrong?” before attackers do.

          In Threat Tiger you draw the system as a data-flow diagram (DFD): processes that do work, data stores that keep data, external entities (users and outside systems you don’t control) and the data flows between them. Trust boundaries mark where data moves between areas with a different level of trust, such as from the internet into your network.

          STRIDE

          For each part of the diagram, consider the six STRIDE categories. Each one is the opposite of a security property you want to keep:

          CategoryPropertyWhat goes wrong
          SpoofingAuthenticationSomeone pretends to be another user, service or device.
          TamperingIntegrityData, code or configuration is changed by someone who should not change it.
          RepudiationAccountabilitySomeone can deny having done something because there is no reliable record.
          Information DisclosureConfidentialityData is exposed to people or systems that should not see it.
          Denial of ServiceAvailabilityThe system is slowed down or stopped for legitimate users.
          Elevation of PrivilegeAuthorisationSomeone gains more rights than they were given.

          Threat Tiger helps with each step: the security switches and boundaries you set trigger concrete threats from a curated library of 601 (with OWASP, CWE and MITRE ATT&CK references, real-world incidents and typical controls). The icon and name of a component count too: a component drawn as a GPU server, a .env file or a WordPress site gets threats for that kind of component.

          Start here

          The screen

          1. Top bar. The model name, You: (your name for the activity log), the Review mode badge when the layout is frozen, the ⟳ git-sync button (once set up), the profile button What are you modelling? and the ☰ menu.
          2. Left panel. Session Meta & Context (title, scope, participants, diagram details; click the heading to collapse it) and the Diagram Component Palette. Hover a palette item for a description; click it to add the shape in the middle of the view, or drag it to where you want it.
          3. Canvas. Your diagram. Page tabs at the top left, the minimap at the top right (if switched on), the title block and legend in a corner.
          4. Canvas toolbar. Undo, redo, zoom in, zoom out, zoom to fit, the format painter (the brush), Save as PNG, the view menu (flat, NE isometric, NW isometric), grid settings and the dark-canvas switch. When two or more shapes are selected, the align toolbar appears above it.
          5. Right panel. Properties of the selected shape or flow, Threat Templates (suggestions for it) and Layers.
          6. Bottom panel. Active Threat Register, Mitigations, Insights and the Activity Log (hidden in the built-in profiles; show it with ☰ → View → Panel tabs).
          Small screensOn a phone or narrow window the panels stack and can be collapsed. Touch works on the canvas: tap selects, drag moves a shape or pans, and a two-finger pinch zooms.
          Start here

          The ☰ menu

          Everything that isn’t drawing lives in the ☰ menu at the top right. It works like a desktop menu: hover or click an item with a ▸ to open its flyout, → / Enter open one, ← / Esc close one level, and ↑ ↓ move inside the current level.

          • Model: Import JSON…, Import Mermaid flowchart…, Export JSON, History…
          • Reports & diagrams: Print report…, Export Markdown report, Export Mermaid diagram.
          • View ▸ Review mode, Title block & legend…, Canvas ▸ (minimap, line jumps, animate traffic, live status), show or hide the left, right and bottom panels, Palette sections ▸, Icon sets ▸ and Panel tabs ▸. View changes are saved into the profile you are using.
          • Build from status file… turns a CSV or JSON list of servers into a diagram (see Build from status file).
          • Settings…, Help (this guide, F1) and About & License (version, licence, credits).
          • Reset canvas… empties the model (a snapshot goes to History first) and Clear all data in this browser… removes everything Threat Tiger stored here.
          The palette

          Threat modelling shapes

          The Threat Modeling section holds the five elements of a data-flow diagram. These are model components: they get STRIDE threats, suggestions and security switches.

          ShapeUse it for
          Process / ServiceAnything that runs code: an application, API, microservice, function, container or job.
          Data StoreAnything that keeps data: a database, bucket, file share, cache, queue or log.
          External EntityPeople and systems outside your control: users, partners, third-party APIs, attackers.
          Trust Boundary ZoneA box around everything with the same level of trust (a network, a cloud account, a device). Zones can be nested; shapes inside belong to it.
          Trust Boundary LineA dashed line, for a boundary that isn’t a box (for example the edge of the internet). Drag its ends; drag the middle handle to bend it.

          How boundary crossings are detected

          TipZones are drawn behind shapes. Shapes inside a zone move with it. In Insights, a component that is outside every zone counts as an entry point for attack paths.
          The palette

          Attack paths & trees

          The Attack Paths & Trees section follows MITRE Attack Flow and attack-defence trees. Threat actor and Crown jewel are ordinary components (an external entity with unauthenticated access, and a data store that handles sensitive data), drawn as a red and a yellow circle badge. To make the crown jewel a target for Insights → Attack paths, select it and tick Crown Jewel in Properties. The other shapes are diagram notation: they get no STRIDE threats and are never data-flow steps in attack paths.

          ShapeMeaning
          Threat actorWho attacks: a criminal group, an insider, a bot.
          Crown jewelWhat they want: the asset worth protecting most. Tick Crown Jewel in Properties to make it an attack-path target.
          Entry pointWhere the attack starts (a phishing mail, an exposed port).
          Attack stepOne action. Pick an ATT&CK tactic (the 14 Enterprise tactics) and optionally a technique ID such as T1566 or T1566.001; both are shown on the shape.
          Asset / targetA system or data the step acts on.
          Condition / outcomeA state that must hold, or the result of a step; mark it Success or Fail.
          AND gateAll children are needed.
          OR gateAny one child is enough.
          GoalThe attacker’s objective, at the top of a tree.
          CountermeasureA defence that blocks or detects a step.
          Choke pointA place many paths pass through: the best spot for a control.
          The palette

          Text items

          ItemWhat it does
          Step ActivityA numbered circle with a text box, to walk readers through a scenario. Set the number with − / +, pick a colour, or Hide Text & Box to show only the circle.
          Comment TextboxA free text note on the canvas (Text Content Details in Properties).
          Canvas HeadlineA title, horizontal or vertical, 16 to 48 px.
          TableRows and columns (up to 30 × 12) with an optional header row and header column and the swimlane colour themes. Edit the cells in Properties; double-click a cell on the canvas to jump to it.

          Text items are not part of the analysis: they get no threats and never count as components.

          The palette

          Data nodes & icons

          One search box at the top of Data Nodes & Icons searches everything in it: the fixed items, the ready-made nodes and every visible icon set (sets load as needed; hidden sets are skipped). It shows a count; Esc clears it.

          • Custom Image / Icon: your own picture. Paste an image address or upload a local file in Custom Graphic Source. Uploaded images are stored inside the model.
          • Infrastructure Node: a server, router or other device drawn as an icon in one of 16 colours. It has no security switches; use a process or store for that.
          • Ready-made nodes (32, in three groups): Network (firewall, WAF, load balancer, API gateway, VPN gateway, IDS/IPS, reverse proxy, DNS, CDN, switch, router, Wi-Fi AP), Security tooling (SIEM, EDR agent, secrets vault, HSM, identity provider, PAM) and Platforms & devices (message queue, cache, object storage, backup, container, Kubernetes, serverless function, AI/LLM model, CI/CD pipeline, Git repository, mail server, workstation, mobile app, IoT device). Each is a real component with the right type and subtypes, so it gets tailored threat suggestions straight away.
          • Icon sets (about 2,000 icons): Devices & security, Security & DevOps brands, Tech & OS logos, and the official AWS, Azure, Microsoft Entra, Google Cloud and Kubernetes icons. Each set loads when you open it. A placed icon shows the icon with its name underneath and is a normal component (data store, process…), so suggestions work. Hide sets you don’t use with ☰ → View → Icon sets.
          Third-party iconsThe icon sets come from AWS, Microsoft (Azure, Entra, Fluent UI), Google Cloud, the Kubernetes project, Devicon and Simple Icons, under their owners’ terms (see About & License). A placed icon is stored in the model, so a model never depends on the packs.
          The palette

          Flowchart items & 3D

          Containers

          • Swimlane Grid Layout: a grid of rows and columns. Drop a node into a cell (it is highlighted while you drag); cells grow to fit their nodes, with padding. Drag a column or row border to resize it, double-click it for the automatic size. Add, remove and rename columns and rows, set the headline and pick a colour theme in Properties.
          • Pool: horizontal lanes with a header each.
          • Vertical Lanes: side-by-side columns, for teams, systems or stages.
          • Group / Frame: a titled box that groups related shapes (not a trust zone).
          • Phases / Timeline: chevron columns for the stages of a process.

          Containers are drawn behind shapes, can be resized, use the swimlane colour themes and carry the shapes inside them when moved.

          Shapes

          ShapeMeans
          Process (Rectangle)A step or action.
          Decision (Diamond)A question with two or more ways out.
          Terminator (Oval)Start or end.
          Data / I-OInput or output.
          DocumentA document or report.
          Manual InputData typed in by a person.
          Preparation (Hexagon)Set-up before a step.
          Connector (Circle)A jump to another part of the chart. As 3D it is a database cylinder.
          Stored DataData kept somewhere.
          Sphere, Cone, Pyramid, Stacked layersThe 3D shapes group: solids in every view. Stacked layers have a layer count (1–10) and a layer thickness.

          Flowchart shapes take any fill, border colour and line width (Properties → Flowchart Shape Style), get all six STRIDE categories like processes, and can change type at any time (Properties → Type) without losing their name, flows or threats. Tick 3D to draw any of them as a solid (see Isometric views & 3D).

          Architecture & process diagrams: C4, UML, BPMN, ERD

          The Architecture & Process Diagrams section has four sub-groups (each can be hidden in a profile). Their text (technology, description, attributes, operations, rows) is edited in Properties → Diagram Text; classes and tables grow to fit.

          GroupShapesIn the analysis?
          C4 modelPerson, Software system, Container, Component, External system. Each has a technology line and a description.Yes: people and external systems are external entities, the rest processes.
          UMLActor, Use case, Note, Package, Class (name, attributes, operations).No: notation only.
          BPMNStart, intermediate and end events, Task, exclusive, parallel and inclusive gateways, Data object.No: notation only.

          Drawing

          Working on the canvas

          To…Do this
          Add a shapeClick a palette item (it lands in the middle of the view) or drag it to a spot. Double-clicking adds just one.
          SelectClick a shape or line. Drag on empty canvas to draw a selection box around several shapes. Esc deselects.
          MoveDrag a shape, or use the arrow keys (Shift for five grid steps). Shapes snap to the grid unless snapping is off.
          ResizeDrag the handle at the bottom-right corner of a selected shape.
          ConnectHover a shape, then drag from one of its connection points to another shape. Esc cancels a connection in progress.
          DeleteDelete / Backspace, or Delete in Properties. It asks first if threats would be deleted with it.
          Copy and pasteCtrl/⌘+C and Ctrl/⌘+V copy the selected shapes with the flows and threats between them. Each paste lands a little further away.
          Undo and redoThe arrow buttons in the canvas toolbar, Ctrl/⌘+Z and Ctrl/⌘+Shift+Z (or Ctrl+Y).
          ZoomThe + / − buttons or the mouse wheel zoom around the centre of the view; Zoom to fit shows the whole page. On touch screens, pinch.
          PanHold the right mouse button and drag, or drag empty canvas with one finger.
          Line up shapesSelect two or more: the align toolbar offers align left, centres, right, top, middles and bottom, and (with three or more) Space evenly across and Space evenly down.
          Copy a lookThe format painter (the brush icon in the canvas toolbar): select one shape (the brush is greyed out until you do), click the brush, then click another shape of the same kind to copy its look: for flowchart, attack-tree and diagram shapes the fill, border, line width and 3D settings; for processes, data stores, external entities and infrastructure the display (card, icon only or circle badge), badge colours and icon colour. Its name, type, icon and security settings are never copied. Double-click the brush to paint several shapes; Esc stops. A click that changes nothing tells you why (a different kind of shape, or the same look already).
          Stack orderProperties → Component Z-Depth / Order: Back, Backward, Forward, Front.
          GridThe grid button: 10, 20 (default), 40 or 80 px, and Snap to Grid on or off.
          Dark canvasThe moon button switches the canvas between light and dark. PNG exports follow it.
          See the whole diagram☰ → View → Canvas → Show minimap: a small map in the top-right corner; click or drag in it to move the view.
          Save a pictureSave as PNG in the canvas toolbar saves the current page (with the title block and legend if they are shown).
          The pen-like brush is the format painterIt does not draw. To draw a line, drag from a connection point.
          Drawing

          Data flows

          A data flow is a line from a source to a destination. Select it to edit it in Properties:

          • Name (what travels, e.g. “Card details”), Source / Destination Endpoint (reconnect the ends; only shapes on the same page are listed) and Target Infrastructure Ports Context (e.g. 443/tcp).
          • Security switches: Encrypted Communication Stream and Authenticated Communication Stream. Unencrypted or unauthenticated flows, especially across a boundary, trigger suggestions and make attack paths riskier.
          • Bi-directional Communication Stream (arrows at both ends), Dashed Line, Line Thickness and Line Display Color (16 colours).
          • Curve Rendering Style: Smooth Curved Spline, Sharp Angled Polyline or Elbow (right angles). Elbow lines find their own way around shapes and update while you move them; trust zones, swimlanes, boundary lines and text are crossed freely.
          • Bend points: click a selected flow to add one, drag a point to move it, click a point to remove it; Clear bend points removes all. (On elbow lines a click adds nothing: their route is automatic, and existing bend points act as waypoints.)
          • Line jumps: where two flows cross, the later one hops over the other. Switch it off in ☰ → View → Canvas.
          • Traffic animation and Status check: see Traffic animation and Live status.
          Drawing

          Properties

          The Properties tab shows only what applies to the selected item. For a component:

          • Type: turn it into another kind (process → data store, rectangle → decision…). Name, flows and threats stay.
          • Component Label with name suggestions for the type, and Detail page: the shape gets a ↗ badge that opens that page (drill-down).
          • Component State: Disable Component Card greys it out and leaves it out of the analysis.
          • Icon (Component Subtype Graphic Icon) from 200+ icons in groups (servers, code, web, databases, security, people, attack & threat, security artefacts, identity & directory…). The icon also tells the threat engine what the component is.
          • Display: Card (box with icon and name), Icon only (name underneath, in the icon colour) or Circle badge (with its own fill and border colours).
          • Security Controls Configuration (the switches below) and Associated Threats.
          • Notes (Architectural Scope Notes), Z-order, Disable Isometric Projection, and Status check.
          • Flowchart shapes add Flowchart Shape Style (fill, border, width, 3D, height); diagram shapes Diagram Text; attack steps their ATT&CK tactic and technique; tables, swimlanes and lanes their rows, columns and themes.

          Security switches

          ComponentSwitches
          ProcessRuns with High System Privileges · Telemetry Logging Enabled · Handles Highly Sensitive Data · Crown Jewel
          Data storeTamper Audit Logging Enabled · Stores High-Value Secret Credentials · Stores PII Account Data · Encrypted At Rest · Handles Highly Sensitive Data · Crown Jewel
          External entityUnauthenticated Access Allowed · Is Privileged User Context · MFA Required · VPN Required
          Data flowEncrypted Communication Stream · Authenticated Communication Stream

          Switched-on properties show as small icons on the shape. A Crown Jewel is a target for attack paths.

          Drawing

          Pages & layers

          Pages

          • The tabs at the top left of the canvas. + adds a page; double-click a tab (or press F2) to rename it; ← →, Home and End move between tabs.
          • While renaming, the × in the tab’s corner deletes the page with its shapes (after asking; undo brings it back).
          • Move selection to… moves shapes to another page. Give a shape a Detail page in Properties to get a ↗ badge that opens it; ◀ goes back.
          • All pages share one threat register, one mitigation list and one set of insights; each page keeps its own trust zones.

          Layers

          • The Layers tab in the right panel. Add layer; click a layer to make it active (new shapes go there); double-click (or F2) to rename it.
          • Hide a layer to declutter, lock it so its shapes can’t be moved, or move the selection to it. Hidden layers still count in the threat analysis, and flow ends never attach to hidden shapes.
          Drawing

          Isometric views & 3D

          The view button in the canvas toolbar switches between 2D Flat View, NE Isometric View and NW Isometric View. The model doesn’t change, only how it is drawn; new flows are sharp (straight segments) in the isometric views.

          • 3D flowchart shapes: tick 3D in Properties. In the flat view the shape is drawn as an extruded solid (a 3D process is a cube, a 3D connector a database cylinder; a 3D decision or terminator is a raised tile); in the isometric views it stands up from the ground. The format painter and quick add carry the 3D look; PNG and print show the same drawing.
          • 3D height: a slider, a number box and Auto (worked out from the shape’s size). Stacked layers also have Layers (1–10) and Layer thickness.
          • Per shape: Disable Isometric Projection keeps a shape (a headline, say) flat in the isometric views.
          Analysing

          Threats & templates

          Select a component or flow and open Threat Templates in the right panel. The list is ranked:

          1. Triggered by your model: security switches, boundary crossings and connected flows, with the reason (for example “unencrypted flow crossing a trust boundary”).
          2. Relevant for this component: recognised from its icon and name (an API, an S3 bucket, an administrator…).
          3. The rest of the library for that element type.

          For each suggestion you can Add it (it then leaves the list), ignore it, or mark it not applicable with a reason, which is kept in the model and the report. Hidden suggestions can be shown again under Hidden.

          • Category Filters: click the STRIDE badges to filter; the search box filters by text; Sort Templates orders them.
          • Add (next to the search) creates your own template: title, STRIDE category, description, typical controls (one per line), references.
          • Load / Save back up the whole template library (every field, including the built-ins you deleted) as JSON, to restore it in another browser.
          Where the threats come fromThe library is threat_templates.json (601 threats with conditions that trigger them). If the file can’t be loaded (for example from file://), the copy embedded in the app is used.
          Analysing

          Threat register

          The Active Threat Register (bottom panel) lists every threat in the model. Click a column header to sort (Severity sorts by severity), click a row to jump to its component, and use the buttons in Actions to edit or delete.

          • Filters: search text, severity, STRIDE category and status (including Not fully mitigated and Needs review).
          • New Threat adds a threat by hand; Export CSV saves the filtered list.
          • Editing a threat: title, STRIDE category, technical description, linked component or flow, remediation status (Open / Unmitigated, Partially mitigated, Mitigated / Resolved), likelihood and impact, and the mitigations that cover it.
          • Needs review: an imported threat with an unknown category or status, or a missing component, is flagged for review instead of being dropped.
          Analysing

          Mitigations

          A mitigation is something you do about one or more threats. In the Mitigations tab, New Mitigation opens a dialog with a title, status (Proposed, In progress, Implemented, Verified, Not applicable), a description of how it is implemented, an owner, a ticket link and the threats it covers.

          • Filter by text or status (Not done yet shows everything that isn’t implemented or verified). Click a row (or press Enter on it) to edit.
          • The register shows each threat’s mitigations; Insights counts Mitigations done and Open threats without a mitigation.
          Analysing

          Insights & attack paths

          The Insights tab sums up the model and what is still missing:

          • Tiles: threats, critical, open critical / high, not fully mitigated, need review, components without threats, rule suggestions, flows crossing a boundary, marked not applicable, ignored, mitigations done, open threats without a mitigation.
          • Open risk heat map (likelihood × impact of the threats that are not mitigated; hover a cell for the count).
          • Open suggestions for the whole model, filtered by component, STRIDE category or reason (from switches, flows and boundaries or from the icon or name), with Add all.
          • STRIDE coverage per component, Model checks (unconnected components, duplicate names, …) and the list of data flows crossing a trust boundary.
          • Attack paths from entry points to crown jewels.

          Attack paths

          Pick a start or target to narrow the list, and click a path to highlight it on the canvas (click again to clear). The Markdown report lists the ranked paths too.

          Presenting

          Review mode

          ☰ → View → Review mode (freeze layout) freezes the layout for a review meeting. Shapes can still be selected, so names, properties, threats and mitigations stay editable, but nothing can be moved, resized, added, deleted, pasted, aligned, retyped or moved to another page; flows can’t be bent or reconnected; the legend is frozen; and undo steps that would change the layout are skipped.

          Review mode is saved with the model, so whoever opens the file sees it frozen too. Click the yellow Review mode badge in the top bar to turn it off.

          Presenting

          Title block & legend

          Open ☰ → View → Title block & legend… (or Settings). The settings are saved with the model and appear on the canvas, in Save as PNG and in print.

          • Title block: the model name and the diagram details from Configure Session Metadata: level (context, level 1–3), status (draft, in review, approved), version, date and author.
          • Legend: a title of your choice, one or two columns.
          • Items on this page: everything the page draws (shape types including 3D variants, icons and cloud icons, flow styles and colours, threat and crown-jewel markers). Tick what the legend shows and edit each item’s text; Reset labels brings the automatic text back. New kinds of items are shown until you untick them.
          • Position: any corner, or Free-floating: drag the legend anywhere (or focus it and use the arrow keys, Shift for bigger steps). It pans and zooms with the diagram. Lock position keeps it in place.

          On screens narrower than 576 px the legend is hidden on the canvas (it is still in the PNG and print).

          Presenting

          Profiles: choosing what the screen shows

          The button left of ☰ asks What are you modelling? A profile decides which palette sections, icon sets, icon-picker groups, right- and bottom-panel tabs and panels you see, and which palette section opens. Your choice is remembered in this browser. Hiding something never changes the shapes on the canvas.

          Presenting

          Settings

          ☰ → Settings… has four sections. The small question mark next to a heading opens the matching page of this guide.

          Title block & legend

          Opens the legend dialog. Saved in the model.
          Profiles

          What each profile shows. This browser only.
          Live status

          On/off switch and interval (this browser), sources (in the model), allowed hosts (this browser).
          Git sync

          Repository settings (in the model) and the encrypted token (this browser).

          Other settings live where you use them: grid size and snapping in the canvas toolbar, the dark canvas, the view mode, panel sizes (drag the edges) and the session metadata in the left panel.

          Live data

          Live status: colour the diagram from real data

          Turn a diagram into a status board: shapes and lines change colour, icon and label from a spreadsheet, a JSON feed or checks the browser runs itself.

          1. Choose where the status comes from

          SourceHow
          Google SheetNames in one column, status in the column to the right (for example Service | Status | Latency with rows like API | up | 120). Share as Anyone with the link can view and paste the share link in Settings → Live status → Add a source → Google Sheet or CSV. Optionally choose the name and value columns by header, letter or number.
          CSV addressAny https:// address that returns CSV, read the same way.
          JSON feedAn https:// address that returns [{"name":"API","status":"up","latency":120}] or {"API":"up"}. Other field names and a path such as data.services can be set.
          Web (HTTPS)A check run by the browser: you get the status code when the server allows it (CORS), otherwise only up or down.
          Reachability (HTTPS)Up or down plus the round-trip time. Browsers cannot send a real ping (ICMP), so this is a timed HTTPS request.
          DNS lookupResolves or not, through DNS-over-HTTPS. The host name is sent to Cloudflare or Google, whichever you choose.

          2. Turn it on for a shape or line

          Select it and tick Status check in Properties (until then nothing changes). Pick the source or check; for a source, the Row name defaults to the shape’s name.

          3. Write the rules

          Rule conditions: equals, not equals, contains (use | for alternatives such as up|ok), < number, > number, latency > ms, latency < ms, no data / error and anything else. Add rule adds one; Default rules restores the defaults for the kind of check.

          4. Test the check

          Test check in Properties → Status check runs the shape’s or flow’s check right away, even with Live status off (hosts still need approval; files on the same site don’t). It shows every part of the answer: up or down, the HTTP status code (or not readable — no CORS), latency, a redirect, the DNS result and IP addresses, or for a Sheet, CSV, JSON or status-file source the matched row with all its columns. It also shows which rule matches now, with a colour preview.

          Each value has an Add rule () button that adds a pre-filled rule, such as equals 503, latency > 950 or equals degraded, so rules are quick to build.

          5. Start it

          ☰ → View → Canvas → Live status (or the switch in Settings) starts checking. It is off by default and remembered in this browser. The first time a host is needed, Settings lists it and asks you to allow it: nothing is contacted before that, so a model from someone else can’t make your browser call addresses you didn’t approve. The refresh interval is 60 seconds by default (at least 10) and can be set per source; Refresh now checks at once; checking pauses while the tab is hidden.

          • Grey means waiting for approval, or data older than twice the interval.
          • State changes such as up → down are written to the activity log.
          • Sources and rules are saved in the model and its exports (a colleague gets them); the results never are.
          Google Sheets: use the share linkA Publish to web link redirects, and redirects are never followed. Use Share → Anyone with the link can view and paste that link.
          Live data

          Build from status file

          Have a list of servers with their status? Turn it into a diagram in one go, and keep it coloured by that list.

          1. Open ☰ → Build from status file…
          2. Give an address (an https:// file, a Google Sheet share link, or a path on the same site such as samples/status-servers.csv) or choose a local file.
          3. Check the Preview, then Build on a new page or on this page.
          4. Leave Keep checking this file for status on to turn on status rules for every shape from its ok, warn, latency and fail columns.

          Loading the file again updates the diagram: new rows are added and existing shapes updated, shapes you placed are never moved, and you are asked before anything is deleted. Files on the same site need no host approval; other hosts must be allowed once (see Live status).

          Sample files

          Download status-servers.csv Download status-servers.json

          Both samples describe the same small server estate. Open one in a spreadsheet or text editor to see the format, change it, and load your copy.

          Columns

          Column names are case-insensitive. Only name is required.

          ColumnMeaningDefault
          nameThe shape’s name (and the row name for status checks). Required.—
          statusThe current status value.empty
          typeprocess, datastore, interactor, infrastructure, or a ready-made node id such as firewall, siem, api-gateway.infrastructure
          iconA Bootstrap icon, e.g. bi-server.the type’s icon
          ok + ok_colorHealthy values, separated by |, and their colour.up|ok|online|healthy|200, green #198754
          warn + warn_colorWarning values and their colour.degraded|slow|warning|maintenance, amber #ffc107
          fail_colorThe colour when no rule matched.red #dc3545
          latency + latency_maxLatency in ms and the limit; above it the shape turns to warning.—
          groupShapes with the same group go into one trust zone.no zone
          connects_toNames of other rows, separated by |: each becomes a data flow.—
          descriptionGoes into the shape’s notes.—

Edge firewall,up,firewall,DMZ,Web 01,,
Web 01,up,process,DMZ,API 01,120,800
API 01,degraded,api-gateway,App,Orders DB,640,500
Orders DB,down,datastore,App,,,

  "items": [

      "type": "process", "group": "DMZ",
      "connects_to": "API 01" },
    { "name": "API 01", "status": "degraded",
      "latency": 640, "latency_max": 500 }

          JSON can also be a bare array of items. Each item uses the same field names as the CSV columns.

          Live data

          Traffic animation

          Select a data flow and, in Properties → Traffic animation, switch on Animate traffic. Choose a Speed (slow, normal, fast) and a Style (moving dashes or moving dots). Traffic runs from source to destination, both ways on a two-way flow; on the light canvas the dashes are white so they show on dark lines.

          ☰ → View → Canvas → Animate traffic pauses every animation (remembered in this browser), and with reduce motion set in your system the lines stay still. PNG exports and printouts show the plain diagram.

          Import & export

          Mermaid (import)☰ → Import Mermaid flowchart…Paste a flowchart / graph: nodes become flowchart shapes, subgraphs trust zones, laid out automatically. Add it next to the current model or replace it (undo brings it back).
          Mermaid (export)☰ → Export Mermaid diagramThe diagram as Mermaid flowchart text. Trust zones become subgraphs; a data flow that crosses a trust boundary (line or zone) is drawn red and labelled with the boundaries it crosses, since Mermaid cannot draw the lines themselves.

          Files & sync

          Git sync with GitHub or GitLab

          1. Create an access token: on GitHub a fine-grained token for the one repository with Contents: Read and write; on GitLab a personal or project token with the api scope.
          2. Fill in ☰ → Settings… → Git sync: service, server (defaults to https://api.github.com or https://gitlab.com; GitHub Enterprise https://host/api/v3), repository (owner/name, GitLab group/subgroup/project), branch (main), file (threat-model.json), the token and a passphrase (8+ characters) that encrypts it.
          3. Connect. Threat Tiger checks that the token can open the repository, then shows the ⟳ button next to ☰.
          4. Press ⟳ to sync. After a reload, the first sync asks for your passphrase.
          5. Optional, a readable copy: tick Also commit a readable copy (Markdown) to also write a Markdown file to the repository (README.md by default, so it is the repository's front page; change it under Readable copy file) that GitHub and GitLab show as a page with the diagram drawn. Under Include in the readable copy choose the sections: Diagram, Risk summary, Threats, Mitigations, Data flows and Components; they are written in that order, like the printed report. It is written fresh on every sync and never read back, so it replaces any file with that name and edits made to it in the repository are overwritten; an unchanged model makes no new commit.
          • The sync settings (not the token) are part of the model and its exports, so a colleague who opens your JSON gets the ⟳ button and only needs their own token.
          • A model can’t redirect sync: nothing is sent to a target until you confirm it with Connect in this browser.
          • Forget token removes the token from this browser; Remove sync from this model removes the settings.
          Files & sync

          History & clearing data

          • History (☰ → History…): snapshots saved automatically in this browser every few minutes, and before imports, restores, resets and deletions of threats. The latest 25 are kept. Restore one to go back; a snapshot of the current model is taken first.
          • Activity Log (bottom panel): what changed, when, and by whom (the name under You:). It is a convenience history, not a tamper-proof audit trail.
          • Two tabs: if the same model is changed in another tab, this tab stops saving and offers Reload or Keep this tab’s version; the other version is kept in History.
          • Reset canvas… empties the model (after a snapshot).
          • Clear all data in this browser… removes every model, snapshot, template change and preference Threat Tiger stored here. Use it on shared machines; export first what you want to keep.

          Reference

          Privacy & security

          • Your data stays in your browser. The model is in localStorage and History in IndexedDB. Nothing is uploaded unless you set up git sync and press ⟳, or turn on live status for hosts you allowed.
          • No trackers, no CDNs. Every library, icon and font is part of the app, so it works offline.
          • Network requests only when you ask: images an imported model references (after asking), git sync to the server you configured, and live-status checks to hosts you allowed. Redirects to hosts you didn’t allow are never followed. DNS checks send the host name to the provider you chose.
          • Tokens for git sync are stored encrypted with your passphrase (PBKDF2 + AES-GCM) and never go into the model or exports.
          • Imported models and templates are untrusted: they are validated and never run as code.
          • Anyone with access to your browser profile can read what is stored there. Use Clear all data in this browser… on shared machines, and keep exported files somewhere appropriate: threat models describe weaknesses of real systems.
          • If you host Threat Tiger yourself, give it its own origin (domain or sub-domain): browser storage is shared by every page on the same origin.
          Reference

          Troubleshooting & FAQ

          I clicked the pen icon and nothing was drawn.

          The brush in the canvas toolbar is the format painter: it copies one shape’s look to another. It is greyed out until exactly one shape is selected. Shapes of the same kind only: two cards with the default look already look alike, so painting them changes nothing (a message says so). To draw a data flow, hover a shape and drag from one of its connection points. Esc leaves the format painter.

          Why can’t the browser ping my server?

          Browsers can’t send ICMP pings. Reachability is a timed HTTPS request instead, so the host must answer on HTTPS. Without CORS headers you only get up/down, not the status code.

          My Google Sheet shows no data.

          Use the Share → Anyone with the link can view link, not a Publish to web link: those redirect, and redirects are not followed. Check that the host is allowed in Settings → Live status and that the row name matches the shape’s name.

          Live status stays grey.

          Grey means the host still needs your approval (Settings → Live status lists it), or the data is older than twice the refresh interval. Is Live status switched on in ☰ → View → Canvas?

          “Open demo model” doesn’t work when I open the file by double-clicking.

          From file://, browsers block the app from reading other files, so the demo, the threat library file, the sample files and the screenshots in this guide may not load (the embedded threat library is used instead). Serve the folder over http (for example npm run serve or python3 -m http.server), or use Import JSON and choose demo.json.

          A palette section or tab is missing.

          The current profile hides it. Pick Show All in the profile menu, or switch it back on in ☰ → View or Settings → Profiles.

          I can’t move or delete anything.

          Review mode is on (yellow badge in the top bar), or the shape is on a locked layer (Layers tab).

          A red banner says my changes are not being saved.

          The browser’s storage is full, usually because of large uploaded images. Export the model as JSON straight away, then remove or shrink the images.

          A notice says the model was changed in another tab.

          Choose Reload to continue with the other tab’s version, or Keep this tab’s version. Either way the other version is kept in History.

          Where is the licence and version?

          ☰ → About & License.

          Press Tab to move between components and data flows, Enter to select, arrow keys to move the selection (Shift for larger steps), Delete to remove it, Escape to deselect, Ctrl or Cmd plus Z to undo.

          Your changes are not being saved. Export the model now so nothing is lost, then remove large images.
          This model was changed in another tab. This tab has stopped saving so it doesn't overwrite those changes. Reload to continue with the other tab's version (this tab's version is kept in History), or keep this tab's version (the other one is kept in History).
          Are you sure?
          Build from status file

          Load a CSV file, a Google Sheet or a JSON file that lists your servers. Each row becomes a shape, groups become trust zones and connects_to becomes data flows. Keep checking the file and the shapes show its status live.

          An https address (asked once per host), a Google Sheet shared as "Anyone with the link can view", or a file on this site (no approval).
          Format help and sample files

          A CSV file or sheet with a header row, or JSON as { "title": "…", "items": [ { "name": "web-01", "status": "up" } ] } (or just the list). Column names ignore case, and _, - and spaces are the same.

          • name (required, unique): the shape's name and the key looked up for its status.
          • status: the value checked, for example up, degraded, down.
          • type: process, datastore, interactor, infrastructure (default) or a ready-made node such as firewall, api-gateway, load-balancer, cache, siem.
          • icon: a Bootstrap icon such as bi-server (default: from the type).
          • ok (default up|ok|online|healthy|200) and ok_color (default green #198754).
          • warn (default degraded|slow|warning|maintenance) and warn_color (default amber #ffc107).
          • fail_color: any other status (default red #dc3545). No data or no row: grey.
          • latency (ms) and latency_max: above the limit shows the warn colour.
          • group: shapes with the same group share a trust zone. connects_to: names separated by |, each a data flow.
          • description: the shape's notes.

          Samples with six servers in different states: status-servers.csv · status-servers.json.
